4. A leech's remedy: for a festering wound, to determine whether it will heal — whether the ailment is in one of the organs, or in the throat, or elsewhere in the body — a salve for this: take a preparation of plants; apply it to the sore; take a swallow of the mixture.
5. A remedy: let the physician take a mouthful of a preparation, rub it about, apply it to the tongue and mouth for soreness; for the same condition, for swelling in the palate: a third remedy.
6. A remedy for toothache: if a worm causes the toothache, and for pain in all the teeth; also for sudden toothache; and for pain in the gums.
7. A remedy if a man vomits blood.
8. A remedy for a swelling: split it and pinch it; apply a poultice, and a good salve.
8. A remedy to stop blood flowing out freely: bind the blood vessel tightly; let it reduce; diminish it; prepare a mixture: combine equal parts.
10. A remedy for a sore joint: if it is inflamed.
11. A remedy for a prolonged illness.
12. A remedy for a shoulder complaint; and a remedy for pain in the kale-stalk [intestines/bowel].

These are medical remedies.
A remedy for swelling of the veins.
A remedy for woad.
Remedies for a cough, how it comes upon a person's body, and how one should treat it. Three prescriptions for a cough, and for shortness of breath, and then for relieving a cough.
Remedies for chest pain — four prescriptions.
Remedies for throat pain — five prescriptions.
Remedies for the great hiccup, and how it comes about — from a weakened stomach, or from excessive heat, or from too much phlegm, or from a harmful temper, or from eating too much moist food — and how one should treat it, a remedy for each condition.
Remedies for a bloated stomach.
Remedies for shoulder pain — three prescriptions.
Remedies for pain in the side and for pain in the flank — pine prescriptions.
Remedies for linden-tree sickness — a prescription.
Remedies for thigh pain — a prescription, and for knee pain thereafter.

4. Remedies for pain of the joints. Tis penso physic.
5. Remedies for shank disease. For the shanks when the limbs of the shin are swollen, a swelling from humors, a splint may help.
6. Remedies for swelling within. If there is inflammation, if the spell of illness comes, or if many pustules arise, to draw out the matter within, to treat it: this is for that condition — all for swollen joints.
27. Remedies for gout. For the condition of the limbs, of the foot if there is swelling, when it has long lasted, six joints.
28. Remedies for backache. Travel and toothache — their joints, have pain.
28. Remedies for many a sting. Take bee-sting remedies, others also — their joints.
30. Remedies for the scalp and for the head. This is for healing with a lotion: that help of the feet.
31. Remedies for every kind of dog bite and also if there is a spell of illness upon the whole body — for each remedy and help: a quick remedy, to treat within the body's afflictions, a strong spell, apply a bandage internally or externally, or for a blow or wound — for each of these things, this is the remedy.

For the body, with suppurations, against swellings, a salve:
of preparations, of the same kind, take with all those of the hen,
suppurations in the palate, apply to that part of the body.
XI. Medical remedies for the pale swollen inflammation: take
a bath, of preparations, against pepper-corns, take
warm to the body, and against sores here and there, take sulfur
put on, take a salve of preparations against skin inflammation
take all against swelling. Medical remedies.
VIII. Medical remedies, of preparations, take sulfur, a small amount, against eruptions
of the sores, eight portions of wolf
If suppuration breaks from a dog's wound, take against the nails
take bread thereon.
XVI. Major medical remedies against eruptions, brass applied to the sores,
for the wounds of the body, anoint them with oil,
how one shall treat this: if it breaks open severely,
take the noble remedy, take it every morning, and let one
take the father's blood as one shall require; if one
shall cut a limb from the trunk; or else if
one must cut within the house; take bread of preparations,
take a salve against the swelling, with oil.
XXVI. Medical remedies against skin disease, for each inflammation that is hot.
End.

Against a festering swelling that is very painful: if a person cannot retain their food, and fails a little, and if they cannot urinate, and if they urinate blood, and if there is danger in those conditions: fourteen remedies.

37. A remedy against when a person cannot retain their food, and if they fail a little, and if they cannot urinate, and if they urinate blood, and if there is danger: fourteen remedies.

38. A remedy for wounds: for a festering swelling, against all wounds, and for each wound on the body, to treat a wound, for a bruise, if there is a swelling in the throat, against a dog's bite, a remedy for lung disease, for an internal wound, a remedy, a half remedy for an inflamed wound, a small wound: if a person is wounded, or struck with a weapon, or beaten with a rod, or if a joint is from a limb, or a snake or a dog has bitten, or if the foot is injured, a remedy for cleansing a wound, a remedy for gathering people together: remedies.

39. Remedies against all kinds of illness, all festering swellings, against conditions coming from outside, against all conditions.

Against all bleeding of wounds. Against all swelling from heat. Against swelling of glands, against all swellings. Against all swellings, this is the recipe.

40. The physician's remedy: a poultice against all swellings of the joints.

51. The physician's remedy against swelling within the joints.

52. The physician's remedy against dysentery. Boil elder-bark together with it. Against swelling, take elder-bark together; against sore muscles and on the body, strain through a cloth and strain again through a cloth of silk.

53. The physician's remedy against pain in the bowels.

54. The physician's remedy against pain inside, that is against rupture; against that which causes pain. Take this and mix it together.

45. The physician's remedy for all manner of ailments. Against pain in the limbs, against bruising, against soreness, against all manner of bodily suffering that a person has, and if any part of the body is swollen; take juice of elderberry and boil it well. Each day take elderberry boiled down, against all ailments; against swelling throughout, against each of all pains; if the head aches, rub on the scalp; against this let the physician know; and let the man be treated.

Let the swelling be entirely [treated] thus: twenty cuttings against the affliction.
46. Remedies against pustules: on the body with wax, scrape open the pustule thereupon. Five remedies there are for this.
47. Remedies against swellings: a salve against a swelling of the thigh; of many kinds of swellings, a preparation against the complaint, and twelve salves against the complaints of the thigh.
48. Remedies against the fume that is inwardly troublesome in a man, and for the condition of the side and flank — twelve salves in all against that affliction.
48. A remedy on a festering sore: against a small pustule.
50. Remedies against a swelling of the hand; a preparation for pain of the hand; wax salve against pain of the hand; six cuttings of salve; four peas.
51. Remedies against pustules that afflict a man's skin.
52. A remedy: a preparation against lice.
53. A remedy: a preparation against smoky pustules.
54. A remedy for a pustule on the body: take a nettle-preparation.
55. A remedy against spreading sores on the body.
56. Remedies against spreading sores on the body; a salve preparation.
57. Remedies: preparations and salves against an itch.
58. Remedies for a painful swelling; for boils.

viii. Remedies for papular eruptions on the skin, a healing draught for the eye; also for nerve pain.
ix. Remedies for a burn or scald: eight preparations.
x. Remedies for a swollen limb; for when a limb is injured; also if a joint pops out of place, and for pain in the limb, preparations to restore it to its place.
xii. Remedies for pimples and eruptions on the body; for pain in the hand; for bruising and sore outgrowths; for every kind of abscess; a linctus for the chest; a preparation for human ailments; for the condition called "onhurl" or lame joints: write the name of the great God, and anoint the affected part with holy water and a holy prayer, and sing over it ten times. Ten remedies.
xiii. Remedies for a swelling of the body; how one should prepare prayers and psalms over the afflicted person; ring the church bell over the afflicted one; for sore muscles; for pain in the throat and chest.
xiii. Remedies for celery-wort preparations; for lung conditions; also an additional remedy involving certain herbs gathered according to kind, and a preparation.

65. A remedy that is for sinew ailment, the names of the herbs, the ones required, the ones needed, of which some of the psalm verses are written five times.
66. A remedy for anointing a wound, and for a swelling.
67. A remedy as a poultice for numbness, with cold water or with milk, three times.
68. A remedy for when a hunting hound bites a man, and for bee-sting, in the name of the angel of the Lord.
69. A remedy for a dog's bite and for a dog's wound. Seven remedies.
70. A remedy for a throat swelling, or a neck swelling.
71. A remedy for a painful abscess, and for a chest disease, roasted.
72. A remedy for whichever disease causes bleeding, for which one applies the Latin words.

Romans — and all the people prepared for him the house against the discomfort of an ailment. And how one may bloodlet: on the sixth day of the waxing moon do not let blood from the lower parts. And then apply a bandage afterward. And if a wound is on the surface, and if you wish to find blood to let, either from a vein, or else if you cannot find the blood of a wound to press out, or else if you cannot find a swollen vein to press, or else if one is to be bloodlet from the shoulder.

xiii. A remedy if any limb is numb.
xiii. A remedy for swellings and pustules on a limb.
xiv. A remedy for watery swellings of the feet and ankles.
xv. A remedy for itching.
xvi. A remedy if a pupil should swell outward in a blister.
xvii. A remedy if one has no desire and there is an eruption.
xviii. A remedy if a man has long-lasting painful swellings.

Remedy 80: A remedy for when a person overdrinks himself.
Remedy 81: A remedy for great cold.
Remedy 82: A remedy if there is excessive [swelling/inflammation] [illegible].
Remedy 83: A remedy for [illegible] of a man.
Remedy 84: A remedy for when a man is stung.
Remedy 85: A remedy for when a man [is afflicted] on some day, against his [body's] affliction of the thigh.
Remedy 86: A remedy if the tongue greatly swells up in the land [of the mouth]; he shall take [this].
Remedy 87: A remedy if a man's scalp peels; if then a man has [illegible].

On this Christian medical practice, these remedies are against all that afflicts the body and spirit.

Poppy — pound it, mix with [illegible], press together; apply the pulp, press it to the [affected] place; smear then with that which has been soaked overnight in vinegar.

For hoarseness of voice: take pennyroyal, pound it thoroughly, mix with pepper and vinegar, let it cool — wash the throat, smear on the same plant rubbed onto the hoarseness — rub well, then turn to the prescribed pills.

For the same condition: take betony and peony, grind thoroughly, tie in a cloth and let it hang; smear on. For hoarseness of voice: bruise a pear, take the thumb-portion, mix with honey and apple juice; set it toward the east facing the rising sun — so that the hoarseness may be driven away throughout the chest. Have oil in the mouth or without; let it run down gently from the uvula; do this frequently until the throat becomes clear.

For hoarseness of voice: take the herb found in the river pool, pound it, blend with ale until it is well soaked; apply to the throat.

For hoarseness of voice: take a whole grain, pound it, mix with nettle-plant, rub it well onto the palate; let it steep on a rough cloth until settled.

About treating the throat with a steam poultice:
For throat pain: take a mallow plant, steep it in water, squeeze it, press it into a linen cloth and wring it out, then lay it warm against the throat.
If the throat aches and swells, scrape it with a razor and apply a poultice to it.
For throat swelling: take agrimony, pound it, rub it with a cloth, then pound it into a poultice and press it against the throat.
If the throat aches: take hops and wine mixed together, smear with honey and apply.
If the throat is sore: take dill blossoms, stand them in oil, apply and rub with that oil.
If it is the same: take the herbs, pound them, mix with vinegar for the throat's soreness, and bind it on the tongue.
If it is the same: take the full prescription, rinse thoroughly, rub to a paste, strain it and apply to the throat.
Apply this salve on the throat as it needs.
If the throat and neck ache: take hardened nettle, cut it up, mix with vinegar, and put it all together and apply.

If one has pain in the head or temples, take pepper, sprinkle it on a sore, apply it with vinegar, bind it up. For honey treatment, take woad juice, press it onto the mouth opening, rub it on the cheeks, it will heal. If one has pain in the head or temples, take pepper, the dove's feather-soft herbs, rub them finely, put vinegar on the sore with that preparation on both sides, then mix with pepper, or take woad seed, grind it on vinegar, smear well with that, rub it on the neck with it. Acne is a sore condition, a kind of swelling that breaks out under the flesh of the arm, or under the armpit, or on both of them. The physician must know from the appearance whether the swelling is ripe or not. When the swollen gland must be opened, he should prepare a lance to lance it and drain it. If this condition has come from great heat, the physician should treat it with cold medicine. If it should be of a cold kind, then the physician should treat it with hot medicine. The physician must take care and mix rightly to restore a man to health. He must take care not to injure him, and not anoint him with bad ointments.

Take a preparation of brooklime and a little of the plant, scrape it from above on that wound and pound it well. And for pain in the side, take a tuneful of self-heal and one need not fear the side-pain too greatly, apply it to the wound and that is the remedy.
For pain in the side, take ground ivy, Jacob's ladder, and wound-wort root, and pounded fennel, a little mint, and betony. Pound all these plants together and drink a cup of the infusion. Seek it for the sinewy pain, seek the tender parts, especially the betony. And if the wound breaks out, take egg yolk and a little honey and apply it to the wound, and lay two leaves over it and bind it around with a cloth for two days. If the wound breaks, and you then want the flesh to heal, and cannot stop it festering, and cannot heal it, then for the pain in the side take wood shavings and pounded fennel and a mixture boiled together, and wipe with a cloth dipped in the liquid, then go in and it will draw out the bone.

Take these or a bath: if the pain or trouble comes through the nose or through the nostrils, look at the sponge in the vessel — it will cause the troublesome thing to descend; it passes through the mouth or through the nose. Then when you must apply it, set the patient lying with the head hanging; take some spittle and rub it; take some of the preparation, select a fine one. Stir it into the salve — that preparation — take vinegar, that herb, the same measure, pound it together to make it softer on the skin. Then pour it on, give it repeatedly: the preparation for the salve, for the palate, for the uvula hanging down.

If a man has a sore spleen: take the herb called elder, of the same — take one part of the same herb, and of the same herb equally — some people call it "lambscress," others call it by another name — a preparation of twenty equal parts together. Collect them all in a vessel with honey. Heat it in the vessel; have it inside for a long time; remove it when it is jelly-like. Then apply the spleen remedy in the summertime; take a good bowl's worth; give it to the patient with great quantity, and you call it thus.

Make a poultice of it and blossom-medicine to wash around, then pour it into the cavity of the hollow plant, and spread it, smear it on the affected area. For a stye on the eye, take half the plant, grind it finely, take half of it, do with it as directed, mix with medicines, frequently anoint with oil of henbane. Again for a stye, take meal, knead it on a flat surface with fat, spread it out, and spit. For a swelling of the neck, take soapy water, prepare a bath with salt, with honey smear it, take a pod of the plant with pursecup, the leech's remedy: if for him the healing pod works, apply it accordingly. For this stye, grind it again, rub it on the affected area, drink it, and mix vinegar and pepper with it, and anoint oil on it, apply the healing pod, and smear with it.

Leech's remedies: of this mixed compound, take celandine sap or blossom, mix it, place it on the diseased area, honey do on it, in a clean flat vessel, apply it over.

For a sore that has festered and is boiled out, this is a good remedy for pain that descends: Take the same plant, pull it from the earth on both sides, mix it with the juice of a plant, a great measure smoothed with a mortar. For pain in many parts of the eyes, that causes one to look dimly and coldly upon things, so that they cannot see clearly, but great pain goes throughout, causing distress; and spittle comes out below, rising from the belly when it is squeezed, so that they cannot digest. But if the bile rises so that the humors are set to flee, and the limbs lie in bed so that the back cannot lie still, bind it that it not slip. These things similar to this, every day will help them together. For pain of mixed kind, a good thorough remedy for that: take thirty niter portions on a young shoot, one that is freshly cut outside, fill it then with thin pitch. After that, put it upon the shoot with the pitch, each day rub it at the appointed time. Also of

For the same condition: take some elecampane and plantain juice with wine, and boil pippin in fire until done. For a wine mixture: take ground mallow root, fine powder of opium, ground parsley, roots of crowfoot, mallow powder, and honey mixed with turmeric; combine all these together and hang in a cloth for a day until ready. Then once the physician sees that the wound is cleansed, apply to the wound a salve of poppy, and grind in mallow powder; let it have its full effect, do so on the eye.
Take elecampane: take balsam and honey, mix with water, a large amount, combine together and apply with that.
For hoarseness of the throat, wash with salt water and pray. Before letting the man loose, apply the throat salve and mix with water; take ointment of palm and balsam with honey, if you have it; make it so that it will heal, in the middle of the night; apply it four times, and let the matter warm up.
For eye mixture: bathe with nettle water and apply; then add pine honey, mixed, and apply.
Take mallow root and rose and grain salve and...

Mix with dicenny and mullein toward the disease, blended together with paragonium. Then take celendine, grind finely and mix with milk, strained through a cloth against coughing.
Take then the mullein, mix it with sinipe.
Take also pine needles, bind them together, press them then, and mix the juice with honey.
Take also the herb vulpam, prepared in warm water, blend it with honey, mix in with sinipe.
For eye disease: take betony herb, prepared with its juice, pound it and squeeze it thoroughly, then take the juice and add to it celandine with a great deal of the mixture strained together, put into the eye. Then take sinulas, pound it thoroughly, mix it with honey. Seethe the herb, then when it has cooled, as long as it is smooth, mix with honey carefully, put it then into a vessel, a flask. Then apply it with the mixture right through until the thick matter is found to be gone.
For eye disease: take celandine herb or hawthorn blossom, pound it, mix it with pure honey, put it on a cloth tile, then lay it in a warm pan or on a hot stone or heat it thoroughly.

Against a sudden affliction: a remedy against loss of a limb.
Some have need of these remedies. To go about with their companions. If the limb is failing, take and make from the juices of certain plants, boil them in a vessel on hot coals, let the man go in, bathed with his companions. If the limb is failing, take a decoction of certain plants, boil with them, so that the swelling of the limb is reduced by the steam. Against a swelling of the ash-plant: take juice of the lily, grind it, mix with the pulp of the plant, steep for several days. When the failing has passed, press it through straining cloth with honey. Apply daily to the hollow of the limb.
Another remedy: if a man becomes afflicted through no fault, having been struck with blows, with sticks, with rods, or if the man is wounded or bruised internally: let him take food easily and lightly, with gentle things internally, so that his bones may recover. Against such internal bruising: a man must address such a fault with vigor. Take pepper and...

When a man applies old medicine, let it stand for a time; then do what is best for the patient. Wash it and let it dry, bind it so it does not wet through the wall of the wound. For a swelling of the glands or jaw-pain: take ox-lip and apply it; boil it in butter.

For a bond or swelling of some kind: take a scraping, collect gall, take some of that compound, mix thoroughly. If it continues, the medicine does not take hold: apply it again over the spot, and let it dry.

For an eye ailment: take celandine, add garlic, take a good amount; crush them together, take pepper, and a good portion of gall; mix them together with garlic; apply over the affected spot; let it stand a night; put it on the eye very carefully; apply it to the lid; let the physician decide the treatment.

For cramps: take nine hollow cups, apply them; set them as strongly as may be needed.

For that condition: boil it for him, say a spell over it, and give him bee-plant, and add more of the same; apply it all upon the affected part; let the breath pass through it.

For a pain in the neck: take the juice of horehound, boil it.

For swollen throat or for swollen jaw, the vapors rise in the mouth and cause trouble in the throat.

For eye pain, take pepper and bind it inside with a coriander seed, boil it in water, put it on the eye.

For eye salve, take nut, coriander, and wheat grain, grind them to dust, put into a strainer, press through cloth, put then on the eye. For eye soreness, take garlic, a piece of bread crumb, and pepper, pound well in a mortar, bind on the eye at night. Thus one shall treat swollen eyes: take pennyroyal, beans, peas, and more, pepper, grind well, wrap in a cloth, bind on the swollen area, let it draw for a time, then set the pan on the eye at night. For swollen eyes, take woodbine, woodbine juice, warm it, pound beans fine, take these seeds, mix the pepper with them, put on the swollen area, or put on the swollen feet, let it stand through the night, or if the swelling has burst, take the seeds, the old ones, apply with pepper on the swollen area, smear with lard.

Apply this then to the painful joint with the poultice, put the ragan below it. Boil the mc paulpe mixed: take spelt, peel the spelt, wash it well and grind it thoroughly, mix with must, grind all to dust, a plaster wrapped around, apply it to the ailing part, keep it on the limb for the time prescribed, anoint with oil of fenugreek mixed with tallow, fasten it on, bind it with clay, squeeze out the juice from the plant, put it in a vessel and let it stand until it separates, drain it, wrap in a cloth, and apply on the wound. Boil cumin and mix with finely ground mustard seed, pour over with fat pine resin, let it drip into a vessel, let it stand until separated, wrap in a cloth, apply under the arm. If the remedy fails, heat it, smear with honey. For a swelling of the liver, take a measure of barley, mix with tallow pressed into balls, in the manner of men, for swelling of the liver take the juice of nettles and smear on the throat, unwrap from the cloth and apply to the body, it will heal. For a swollen tendon: take agrimony leaf, cut finely, press out the juice, mix the flour with it. For a hoarse cough: take ribwort plantain, grind it to meal.

For pain in the joints: take the bark of the bole, scrape it from the elder; take the elder leaves, pack them together, strain; apply to the shoulder; then wipe over with a cloth; then wring over it; let each of the leaves steep a time on the pack.
For swelling of the joints when a man has eaten too many hot, acrid things from the land: take yellow flag and michaelmas herb and fumitory and pennyroyal.
After this swelling, if the houghs of the legs are unsound, apply warmth with a poultice to the eyes.
For a hoarse throat: take a handful of mallow root, of horsetail; boil together until it is well boiled and strained; bathe with it warm.
For one who has hiccups: take hyssop, put it in oil and take it fasting; take celery and bishopwort and alexanders and tutsan and springwort and English moneywort, and

For this illness, take a preparation for all ailments of the throat, a remedy for the disease of the tongue — if the gums are sore on either side, or if there is swelling, or pain in the chin — take sulfur for this ailment.

For a swelling of the throat, take a remedy: boil it in a pan with wine and let it stand. Then take it with a cloth soaked in the mixture and apply it to the throat. Take elm, and mix it with the preparation, and apply it to the afflicted area. Place this on the throat for the disease.

For an ailment of the chest, take a remedy: gather a hundred bunches of herbs, mix them small, and rub them onto the chest over the ribs.

Apply on the wound. For the same condition, take fresh honeycomb, melt it, then put a cloth on the wound and drip it on. For the same condition, take oil mixed with also a hollow stalk, pour it on so that the breath passes away. For the same condition, take henbane seed, put a cloth on the wound, drip it on so the medicine is absorbed. Take bishopwort, elecampane, gyp[sywort], pepper, [and] pennyroyal, comfrey, [and] taper-root, pounded small together with [them]; eight measures of mustard. So prepare this so that the whole [remedy] may be drunk. Nothing harms [the person] if the lungs are diseased. So that the whole [remedy] may completely restore the person to health. This is good against all manner of costiveness:
Take bishopwort, elecampane, hens[bane], savory, blue [herb], clover, pimpernel, southernwood, mugwort, wormwood. Prepare all [these] — boil them all together until completely [reduced]. Eight measures of mustard.

Treat this bone with a bone bandage, and above the shoulders above the arm. Have this wound bathed warmly. Cry out to Paul, that God relieve this swelling and help if one should be lent to relieve this: take a full oven of coals and of the hot embers something, and take the loaf that has been hallowed. Prepare it. And take some clay and some drink of fine ale. And when he has bathed him smooth the swelling. And then soon he will be able to pass the stone out through the urine. Take a decoction: boil it with barley drink, and cool the drink, and take it again morning and noon and evening. And among these plant medicines, the best lasting remedy: take of these herbs a clear portion and prepare a drink of it with salt to drink. Take a pipe and pass it through the urine. Take some of the plant, grind it moderately into a poultice and celebrate a mass and boil morning again; and prepare the whole herb plant and rub a little of the herb material morning with much. Put all these herbs very finely, and press them hard into all the ale and let it stand overnight.

For pain of the lungs:
If the throat is very sore, take nettles, gather them, and peony, and libcorn leaf or anise, boil them with some water, and give to drink; for soreness of the lungs. Chapter XLII.

If a person drinks something, and a loathsome thing sticks in the throat, take a bird feather and make a swab, put it into the throat where the thing is stuck, so that he may vomit it forth; if he cannot get it up by himself, and it cannot be brought up by force, use gall. Chapter XLIV.
Against lust, give him a drink of cold water; if he often suffers from uncontrolled desires. Chapter XLV.
If a wound or swelling: take nettles, put them on the wound so that it soon heals. Chapter XLVI.
Take a fine comb, run it through the hair, and take the combings, steep them in water, and give the person to drink if he will. Chapter XLVII.
For lung sickness: if the mouth is foul or painful, take veal, grind it with milk, give it as a poultice.

This is a remedy. Take three pennyworths of cellandine, and pound it; take pith of elder and milk, and bathe with it the affected limb, then bind the cloth around it firmly and wrap it warmly. Press it then with a bandage. And take broom and elm-rind, and ivy-rind, and apuldram-rind, iris-rind, all the plants that grow in marshy ground: heartswort, sinew-wort, elfwort, buttercup, mayweed, betony, agrimony, and scraped bark; pound the roots all together well and blend them. When the sinews shrink and are pulled, give the patient this drink dissolved in warm water, as much as he can take, so that he can move. Bathe him with these bandages and compresses as much as he can endure. When the patient is so afflicted, lay him in bed completely, and let the swellings fly away. Give him a drink of this prescription with warm water, or with warm mead. Give him then a poultice of all these gathered plants, bound about his painful limbs. Wash his head with cold water. Let blood from him every five nights by the waning moon, fourteen or twenty times. Forty-eight.

Drink for eye disease: take a measure, boil in lukewarm water, let it simmer in the throat region. Take elder bark and saliva combined, and as much as will fit, do not let it stand; do not add any liquid. Strain it and let no foreign matter touch it. Prepare it so that it cannot escape; strain it so that the vessel does not fall and spill; if it burns the eye, leave it; let it not harm; take it again as before. If he cannot be healed by that, take once more the remedy until it ceases and he is relieved.    XL VIII
For a woman's swelling: take a good measure of betony in ale, give it to drink, let it take effect, smear it on gently at the point of the wound.    L

Smear well with grease, wrap the wounds with a cloth soaked in oil. Chapter LIII.
Take a clove of garlic, bind it downward, when it has shriveled, take then lovage and watercress, and pound it well, lay it on. Chapter LIIII.
Boil aloe for three nights until it becomes thick; take birch bark, elecampane, and mix with bishopwort and place it on, smear it on, and it will be healed. Chapter LV.
If the head becomes swollen and the glands are enlarged, take then a pound of oakgall, let it stand overnight in water, then take the boiled liquid and lay a cloth soaked in it about the neck, and let it remain overnight. Chapter LVI.
If a man cannot digest his food, take a pound of celandine, pepper, garlic, laurel berries, and wine. Chapter VII.
If a man cannot make water, let him seek a physician. Chapter LVIII.
For swelling of the tongue: take a plant called polium, soak it in hot water, blow it into the mouth so the head swells not; a man cannot speak until the swelling goes down.

Take a good amount of elderberry juice, the tongue of a bull, and sinew, well ground; add celery, brooklime, leek, and garlic; pound them well together and cook them down in oil until reduced; press out through a cloth and let it stand three nights. Then take the same preparation with the juice of sinew; it shall be good for the tonsils. Chapter 61.

For use as a gargle and for a man who has lost his voice due to disease: take a good quantity of elecampane root, wild celery seed, carrot, bee's wort, harewort, haw berries, black pepper, garlic, leek, hedge berry, grain, gravel root, fennel; pound and boil in water until well reduced; take eight measures, half an apple on birch bark; then strain it and consecrate it with a holy prayer; give it to the sick person divided into portions; keep it a while for the tongue of those who are ill.

Or if it will not diminish, find this plant — smaller than paul's [herb] — his body is afflicted, so the remainder will relieve him. Section 62.
For elf-disease, which is not easy to cure: fennel, oil and such, elder's drink to strengthen. Let God's name be spoken and make incantations and put them all together. Bind them all; prepare it in the prescribed manner. Apply the holy ointment. Let it be taken three times. Mix with myrrh and all seeds. Or if there is a joint ailment, apply it within. Make an application of the angled plant. Purge with these remedies. In the morning before anything, take a little of the prepared mixture. Speak over it the holy name. Anoint the healer's hands. The lord of the holy kind, by these ointments and by God's preparation, let it be within, and this remedy shall be good for the liver. For swelling of the joints, take the plant of the sunny southerly kind, let it stand in the running water in the morning. Let the mixture be well made, and take it as a warm drink. Apply it each day, and take it before sunrise. Also take oak-rind, for the glory of God he commanded this remedy. And whatever pleases him may it be granted.

Against coming again of disease, or so that the swelling may not rise to the throat: take thyme, he dwells under it, and with marsh-wort and with benediction. Say the Lord's Prayer and the Litany of the apostles. The priest shall let the physician go forth, and with the holy one, gathered from the surrounding place, he shall sing the Lord's Prayer. Then sing glory in the highest and sing over him the Litany, and circle around him with a staff four times. Lay him on his side. Then the priest shall command again that the people pray. Then lay the priest to sing eight times the psalm with holy words. Three times take the head of leek and garlic at a given time, and none more than three, and elecampane. In the month following, the fullness of the moon, with the holy words of remedy, be prepared for when he is taken from the feast. In the middle three portions from each side, when he intends it. Have oil with it, putting it toward the left side. Mix it with fat. Then go round about and press the bone together then when he goes to the privy, go three portions toward the left.

And in the place of plague, and Paul's church, and have the patient sound, lay down songs for him, for the holy one, above each piece cut off. And pieces inward, within, do his nine months and nine nights, his navel cord. If he is elf-sick, he shall be barley-cure, though he needs to be scarified. If you then encounter a lame man, set Christ's sign over it, and pray with leaves of haw. If there is a wounded man, and load upon him as you first do at the poultice, and plaster his stool-black. The one whom the physician cannot cure entirely. If he is high in pain, if there is this, and load now upon him as you first do at the poultice, and plaster, his wound shall be treated by the physician. If the wound festers, the swelling by then, six months, and afterwards if the physician cannot then cure him better at all, nor can anything relieve the physician. Pray this prayer: to the lord Jesus, by penance, by penitence, of the lips he says, Amen, Amen, Amen. Lord, Lord, Lord. Lord of Sabaoth. Amen, Alleluia. May the Lord from his grace, in the name of Christ, may the almighty pardon all sins of Jesus Christ; let us be freed from the bondage of the servant of yours. Lord, in your steadfast fortress, worthy of praise, worthy of prayer.

These remedies for internal [ailment]: a drink for sores within, if there be [illness]: silch — take quinces, sing prayers upon it, apply it.
In thy name give me peace.     Chapter 65.
If there is a condition that has been brought about, to cause the eye to run, to remove [it], as has been said, to anoint around the swelling, if it can help to strengthen [it], to prevent loss of vision, make a preparation: pennyroyal, pellitory, self-heal, a portion of honeysuckle, to find a remedy, then heat the salve, apply with warm milk, each time, put on the poultice five times — cut pieces, having great strength against [infection], each [application] softly — drink, drink, [the preparation] acts upon [the wound], [the healer says]: if a wound is festering inside with old matter or with this pennyroyal, anoint around where it aches, with a preparation of elecampane, let the woman attend to it.
